notes.meaning: Moses finished setting up the tabernacle, then anointed and consecrated it, its altar, and all its furnishings. Consecrating something means setting it apart as holy for God's special service. The phrase 'on the day' refers to the general time when the sanctuary was finished and dedicated. God's presence claimed every part of the sanctuary as his own before worship began.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern scholars note that taking the date literally places this event before the census in chapter 1, suggesting that an editor combined separate records or that the Hebrew phrase simply means 'at the time.'

notes.meaning: The twelve tribal chiefs, who had recently helped Moses count the people, came together to present a joint offering. They gave six covered wagons and twelve oxen to help transport the tabernacle through the wilderness. These leaders used their wealth and influence to supply practical equipment for God's work. Leaders ought to be the first to support God's service.

The Lord told Moses to accept the wagons and oxen from the tribal leaders. He commanded Moses to hand them over to the Levites according to the specific needs of their work. God welcomed these willing gifts and directed that they be put to practical use in his service.

Moses obeyed the Lord's instructions and took the carts and oxen from the leaders. He distributed them among the Levites to ease their labor as the nation prepared to move. God cares about the strength and needs of those who serve him.

Moses assigned two wagons and four oxen to the Gershonite clan to carry the curtains, ropes, and fabric coverings. He gave four wagons and eight oxen to the Merarite clan because they had to haul the heavy wooden frames, posts, and metal bases. Ithamar, the son of Aaron the priest, supervised both groups. God divides help wisely, giving the most support where the load is heaviest.

Moses gave no wagons to the Kohathite clan. They were responsible for the most sacred items, such as the ark of the covenant, which had to be carried on their shoulders using poles. Carrying these holy objects by hand showed deep reverence and protected them from being damaged in a wagon.

The tribal leaders brought gifts to dedicate the newly anointed altar for regular sacrifice. The Lord told Moses that only one leader should present his offering each day. Spreading the ceremony over twelve days gave each tribe its own time to honor God and kept the tabernacle court from becoming crowded.

Nahshon, the leader of the tribe of Judah, brought his offering on the first day. Judah received the place of honor because God had stationed them at the front of the camp on the east side. This prominent role also reflected God's ancient promise that Judah would hold the royal scepter.

Nahshon presented a large silver platter and a silver bowl, both filled with fine flour mixed with olive oil for a grain offering. He also gave a small gold dish filled with fragrant incense. These precious dishes furnished the altar with the proper vessels needed for daily worship.

Nahshon brought a bull, a ram, and a lamb as a burnt offering to show total dedication to God. He added a male goat for a sin offering to ask for forgiveness, along with twenty-two animals for a peace offering. The peace offerings provided a large sacred feast for the priests, the leaders, and the people to share together in God's presence.

On the second day, Nethanel, the leader of the tribe of Issachar, brought his gifts. Issachar was camped beside Judah on the east side of the tabernacle, so they followed next in line. The tribes approached the sanctuary in an orderly way that matched their camp arrangement.

Nethanel offered a silver platter and a silver bowl, both filled with flour and oil for grain offerings. He also presented a gold dish weighing ten shekels and filled with sweet incense. His gifts matched the dishes brought by Judah the day before.

Nethanel provided three animals for a burnt offering, a male goat for a sin offering, and seventeen animals for a peace offering. His gifts were identical in kind and amount to the gifts from the first day. This exact equality showed that every tribe had the same standing and the same duty before the Lord.

On the third day, Eliab, the leader of the Zebulunites, stepped forward with his offering. Zebulun was the third and final tribe stationed in the eastern camp under the banner of Judah. God gave each tribe its own turn to participate fully in the dedication.

Eliab brought a silver platter and a silver bowl, both filled with fine flour and oil for a grain offering. He also gave a ten-shekel gold dish filled with incense for the holy place. Zebulun gladly contributed the same valuable metal vessels as the previous leaders.

Eliab brought three animals for a burnt offering, one goat for a sin offering, and a group of oxen, rams, goats, and lambs for a peace offering. Scripture records his offering word for word, showing that God pays close attention to each gift brought in faith. The people celebrated their peace with God through another day of fellowship and thanksgiving.

On the fourth day, Elizur, the leader of the Reubenites, came forward to present his offering. Reuben led the second division of tribes, which was pitched on the south side of the tabernacle. The dedication continued smoothly from one camp division to the next.
